title: Hope
hook: hope is not optimism but confidence in God's promise

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith: pistis, trust, a gift that can grow, even alongside doubt. Your line was trust. When the worry came back, did you open a hand? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

The city has fallen. The walls are down, the streets are empty, and the poet who wrote the Book of Lamentations doesn't pretend otherwise. For two long chapters and into a third, he weeps. He says God has walled him in, made his chains heavy, shut out his prayer. There is nothing in sight to be optimistic about. And then, right in the middle of the book, the voice turns. Not because anything outside has changed. The rubble is still there. He turns because he remembers something. That turn is today's virtue, the second of the three. Hope.

Here's what he remembers, in the King James Bible: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Notice where his hope comes from. Not from the news. Not from a feeling that things are looking up. From God's character, and God's promise. That's the difference between optimism and hope as Christians speak of it. Optimism reads the situation and expects it to improve. Hope can read the same situation, see no improvement at all, and still lean forward, because it rests on who God is. Paul puts it bluntly in Romans: "hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?" If you can already see it, you don't need hope. Hope is for the dark stretch. Then the letter to the Hebrews gives hope its picture, the one in today's line: "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast." Think about what an anchor does and doesn't do. It doesn't stop the storm. It doesn't calm the water. It holds the ship in place while the storm goes on, so the ship isn't driven onto the rocks. Hope, in this picture, doesn't make the night shorter. It keeps you from being carried off by it.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name a hope. Settle, and breathe. Find one thing you're waiting for that you can't see yet: someone's healing, a reconciliation, a change in yourself that's slow in coming. Don't measure the odds. Just name it, quietly, in one sentence. Then rest your breath on it, the way an anchor rests on the seabed: heavy, still, holding. If you pray, you can borrow the poet's words: this I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. The bell holds the time.
Hope. In the New Testament's Greek, elpis. Not a forecast that things will improve, but a confident leaning on God's promise in the dark.
Your line: hope is an anchor. Today, when the news or the day pulls hard, say the hope you named under your breath, and hold your ground for one minute. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Christians speak of hope as confidence in God's promises rather than a prediction; Lamentations 3:22–23 is sung in some churches as the hymn 'Great Is Thy Faithfulness', and some Christians use the anchor of Hebrews 6:19 as a symbol of hope.

fork.setup: you're the poet of Lamentations. your city is in ruins, and you've wept through chapter after chapter. nothing outside has changed. what comes next?
options: keep writing grief to the very end.
insist things aren't really so bad.
remember God's mercies, and hope anyway.
fork.reveal: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope." the rubble stays, and the turn comes from memory, not from the view.

original.note: Greek: hope, the word in Hebrews 6:19 and in Paul's faith, hope and love.

trapdoor: what you thought: hope means thinking things will work out.
what it means: confidence in God's promise that holds even when nothing looks better.
what a scholar hears: the turn in Lamentations 3 comes in the middle of a book of laments over a fallen city, with no rescue in view.

notes: Lamentations 3:1–20 paraphrased: walled in (3:7, 'hedged me about'), heavy chain (3:7), prayer shut out (3:8). 'Right in the middle of the book' describes chapter 3 of five; confirm, and confirm 'the poet' (traditional attribution to Jeremiah not claimed).
Optimism vs hope distinction is the index's; presented as how Christians speak of hope, not as a quoted definition.
howItsDone: the hymn 'Great Is Thy Faithfulness' (Chisholm) is named but not quoted; the anchor as an early Christian symbol of hope (catacomb art) is stated as 'an old Christian symbol'; confirm.
Original: ἐλπίς, el-PEES (or EL-pis in Erasmian pronunciation); confirm.
